properties.name: Addicks Estates
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — UNDERCOUNTED COMMUNITY: Addicks Estates residents live east of I-495, directly adjacent to the Citisteel contamination site (343 acres), I-495, and the new transit center. But their census block group extends north all the way to the PA border, swallowing the entire uninhabited industrial waterfront along the Delaware River. This dilutes the pollution burden score and caused DelDOT to miss this neighborhood in the EFA designation entirely. Real cumulative burden is likely much higher than scores shown. CC4EJ position: Addicks Estates warrants its own census block group for accurate EJ assessment. This gap should be raised in any DNREC permit review affecting this area.

properties.name: Aniline Village
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — UNDERCOUNTED COMMUNITY: Aniline Village is named after the National Aniline Chemical plant, established here in 1914. In 1921, National Aniline merged with four other companies to form Allied Chemical & Dye Corp — which became Allied Signal, then Honeywell, and is now Solstice Advanced Materials, the current owner of the AWE Superfund site immediately adjacent to this neighborhood. Residents of Aniline Village have lived next to the industrial successor of the company that named their street for over a century. Today the neighborhood has a large Spanish-speaking population. Their linguistic isolation burden — a key EJScreen vulnerability indicator — is being hidden by a census block group that lumps Aniline Village with Hickman Road and Knollwood/Worthland. Communities where residents speak limited English have reduced ability to participate in permit hearings, access health information, and advocate for themselves. This boundary failure means DNREC's permit review tools systematically undercount this community's vulnerability. CC4EJ position: Aniline Village warrants its own census block group designation.

properties.name: Hickman Road
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — NATIONAL REGISTER OF HISTORIC PLACES (2006): Hickman Row was built around 1919 by Worth Steel Corporation to house its Black workforce. Residents were families from the Great Migration — people who fled Southern racism seeking economic opportunity in industrial Delaware. The neighborhood's back lots were designed large enough to raise vegetables and livestock. In September 1952, 12 Hickman Row students became the first African Americans to legally integrate a public school in any of the 17 states that allowed segregation — a cornerstone case later cited in Brown v. Board of Education. When Worth Steel sold the properties in 1962, many families stayed. Today Hickman Row sits in the same census block group as Aniline Village and Knollwood/Worthland — three communities with entirely different histories averaged into a single EJ score. A community that helped end school segregation in America deserves to be counted accurately. CC4EJ position: Hickman Road warrants its own census block group designation. Historical marker NC-162, Delaware State Archives.

properties.name: Knollwood / Worthland
properties.note: ⚠ DATA GAP — UNDERCOUNTED COMMUNITY: Knollwood, also known as Worthland, takes its name from Worth Steel — the same company that built Worth Steel's mill in 1916 and constructed Hickman Row for its Black workforce in 1919. The neighborhood has a significant Spanish-speaking population whose linguistic isolation burden is being masked by a census block group that averages three distinct communities — Knollwood, Aniline Village, and Hickman Road — into a single EJ score. A community where residents cannot easily read permit notices or attend English-only public hearings faces a compounded barrier to environmental protection. The name 'Worthland' is a direct trace to the industrial company whose legacy now surrounds this neighborhood as contaminated land and active cleanup sites. CC4EJ position: this block group should be split to accurately represent these three distinct neighborhoods.
